title: Βοὴ ἐπὶ τάφρῳ καὶ ἀγορὴ Τρώων
titleEn: The Shout at the Ditch and the Trojan Assembly — Iliad 18.202–309
part: The Shout at the Ditch and the Trojan Assembly (18.202–309)
about: Athena puts the aegis on Achilles’ shoulders, crowns his head with a golden cloud and kindles a flame from it. He goes to the ditch but, heeding his mother, does not join the Achaeans; he shouts, Athena’s voice joins his, and the Trojans are thrown into confusion, their horses turning the chariots back and twelve of their best men dying. The Achaeans drag Patroclus out of range and lay him on a bier, and Achilles follows it in tears. Hera sends the unwilling Sun down early, the fighting stops, and the Trojans meet in assembly on their feet, too frightened to sit. Polydamas urges them to go back into the city tonight and stand on the walls at dawn, since Achilles will not be able to storm the town. Hector, scowling, answers that they have been shut in long enough, that Zeus has now given him glory at the ships, and that no one will obey Polydamas. He orders supper and a watch, and says he will face Achilles in the morning and stand his ground, for war is shared alike and kills even the killer.

sentences.t:
ἣ μὲν ἄρ’ ὣς εἰποῦσ’ ἀπέβη πόδας ὠκέα Ἶρις,
αὐτὰρ Ἀχιλλεὺς ὦρτο Διῒ φίλος·
sentences.l:
She, indeed, then so having spoken went away, swift-in-feet Iris,
but Achilles rose up, dear to Zeus;
sentences.i: So she spoke, and Iris, swift of foot, went away; and Achilles, dear to Zeus, rose up;
sentences.n: The first line is the same as 8.425, where Iris also goes away after delivering a message, so its English is the same. ὦρτο is the aorist middle of ὄρνυμι ‘rouse’, here ‘rose up’. Διῒ φίλος ‘dear to Zeus’ is a stock phrase, translated every time.

sentences.t:
ἀμφὶ δ’ Ἀθήνη
ὤμοις ἰφθίμοισι βάλ’ αἰγίδα θυσσανόεσσαν,
ἀμφὶ δέ οἱ κεφαλῇ νέφος ἔστεφε δῖα θεάων
χρύσεον, ἐκ δ’ αὐτοῦ δαῖε φλόγα παμφανόωσαν.
sentences.l:
and around, Athena
on his mighty shoulders threw the tasselled aegis,
and about his head a cloud she set as a crown, heavenly-one of goddesses,
golden, and from it kindled a flame all-shining.
sentences.i: And Athena threw her tasselled aegis about his mighty shoulders, and she, heavenly even among goddesses, set a golden cloud as a crown about his head and kindled from it an all-shining flame.
sentences.n: Athena arms the unarmed Achilles with light, as Iris had told him to show himself without armour. ἀμφὶ … βάλ’ is one verb split in two (tmesis), ‘threw around’, and βάλ’ is the unaugmented aorist βάλε; ἐκ … δαῖε ‘kindled out’ is split the same way. θυσσανόεσσαν ‘tasselled’ is the house word for the aegis. οἱ is ‘his’ (the dative of the pronoun), and νέφος ‘cloud’ is what she sets about his head, ἔστεφε ‘put round as a wreath’. δῖα θεάων ‘heavenly even among goddesses’ is a stock phrase for a goddess, with θεάων the epic genitive plural; χρύσεον ‘golden’ goes with νέφος, and αὐτοῦ ‘it’ is the cloud.

sentences.t:
ὡς δ’ ὅτε καπνὸς ἰὼν ἐξ ἄστεος αἰθέρ’ ἵκηται
τηλόθεν ἐκ νήσου, τὴν δήϊοι ἀμφιμάχωνται,
οἵ τε πανημέριοι στυγερῷ κρίνονται Ἄρηϊ
ἄστεος ἐκ σφετέρου·
sentences.i: As when smoke rises into the upper air from a town on an island far away, an island that enemies are fighting around, while its men fight it out all day long in hateful war from their own town;
sentences.n: A simile begins: ὡς δ’ ὅτε … ‘as when …’, answered by ὣς in line 214. The subjunctives ἵκηται and ἀμφιμάχωνται are the ‘whenever’ subjunctives of similes. αἰθέρ’ is the accusative of αἰθήρ, the bright upper air, and ἄστεος is the epic genitive of ἄστυ ‘town’. δήϊοι ‘enemies’ is the adjective δήϊος ‘hostile’ used as a noun. κρίνονται Ἄρηϊ, literally ‘are decided by Ares’, is the idiom for fighting it out, with Ares standing for war. πανημέριοι means ‘for the whole day’, and σφετέρου ‘their own’. οἵ τε begins a new subject: the men of the besieged town, who fight from their own walls, not the enemies around the island.

sentences.t:
ἅμα δ’ ἠελίῳ καταδύντι
πυρσοί τε φλεγέθουσιν ἐπήτριμοι, ὑψόσε δ’ αὐγὴ
γίγνεται ἀΐσσουσα περικτιόνεσσιν ἰδέσθαι,
αἴ κέν πως σὺν νηυσὶν ἄρεω ἀλκτῆρες ἵκωνται·
sentences.l:
and with the sun having set
beacon-fires blaze, close-set, and upward the glare
becomes, darting, for the dwellers-around to see,
in case with ships they may somehow come as warders-off of ruin;
sentences.i: and when the sun has set, beacon-fires blaze close together, and the glare shoots upward for the neighbours to see, in case they may somehow come with ships to be a defence against ruin;
sentences.n: The besieged signal for help. ἠελίῳ καταδύντι ‘with the sun having set’ is a dative phrase with an aorist participle (ἠέλιος is the epic form of ἥλιος). ἐπήτριμοι ‘close-set’ goes with the beacons, and ἀΐσσουσα ‘darting’ with the glare. περικτιόνεσσιν is ‘those who live round about’, with the epic dative ending -εσσιν. αἴ κεν … ἵκωνται is ‘in case they should come’. ἀλκτῆρες ‘warders-off’ is the noun of ἀρῆς ἀλκτῆρα at 18.100; ἄρεω is a genitive that can be read either as ἀρή ‘ruin’ or as Ἄρης ‘war’, and ‘ruin’ is followed.

sentences.t: ὣς ἀπ’ Ἀχιλλῆος κεφαλῆς σέλας αἰθέρ’ ἵκανε·
sentences.l: so from Achilles’ head a blaze reached the upper air;
sentences.i: so from the head of Achilles a blaze reached the upper air;
sentences.n: The simile closes with ὣς ‘so’, and αἰθέρ’ ἵκανε answers αἰθέρ’ ἵκηται of line 207. σέλας is a blaze of light, and ἵκανε is the unaugmented past of ἱκάνω ‘reach’. The comparison is between smoke and glare from a besieged town and the flame from Achilles’ head.

sentences.t:
στῆ δ’ ἐπὶ τάφρον ἰὼν ἀπὸ τείχεος, οὐδ’ ἐς Ἀχαιοὺς
μίσγετο·
sentences.l:
He stood at the ditch, going from the wall, and among the Achaeans
he did not mingle;
sentences.i: He went from the wall to the ditch and stood there, and did not mingle with the Achaeans;
sentences.n: Achilles does what Iris told him to do at 18.198: he goes to the ditch (τάφρος, the trench before the Achaean wall). στῆ is the aorist of ἵστημι ‘stand’ without the augment (Attic ἔστη). μίσγετο is the imperfect middle of μίσγω, the same verb as Attic μείγνυμι ‘mix’, and οὐδ’ ἐς Ἀχαιούς means he did not go into their midst. The reason follows in the next unit.

sentences.t: μητρὸς γὰρ πυκινὴν ὠπίζετ’ ἐφετμήν.
sentences.l: for his mother’s shrewd command he respected.
sentences.i: for he respected his mother’s shrewd command.
sentences.n: The γάρ gives the reason for staying apart: the command of Thetis, in the previous part, that he not enter the fight until she brings new armour. ὠπίζετ’ is the imperfect middle of ὀπίζομαι ‘regard, respect’. πυκινός is literally ‘close-packed’ and of counsel ‘shrewd’; ἐφετμήν ‘command’ is the accusative of ἐφετμή.

sentences.t:
ἔνθα στὰς ἤϋσ’, ἀπάτερθε δὲ Παλλὰς Ἀθήνη
φθέγξατ’·
sentences.l:
There standing he shouted, and apart Pallas Athena
raised her voice;
sentences.i: Standing there he shouted, and Pallas Athena, apart from him, raised her voice;
sentences.n: ἔνθα στάς ‘standing there’ has στάς, the aorist participle of ἵστημι. ἤϋσ’ is ἤϋσε ‘shouted’, printed with the diaeresis as the edition has it. ἀπάτερθε ‘apart’ puts Athena at a distance from Achilles; the two voices are separate. φθέγξατ’ is the aorist of φθέγγομαι ‘utter a sound’.

sentences.t: ἀτὰρ Τρώεσσιν ἐν ἄσπετον ὦρσε κυδοιμόν.
sentences.l: and among the Trojans she roused a boundless uproar.
sentences.i: and she roused a boundless uproar among the Trojans.
sentences.n: ἐν … ὦρσε is one verb split in two (tmesis), ‘roused in’. ὦρσε is the aorist of ὄρνυμι ‘rouse’, the verb of ὦρτο in line 203, here transitive. κυδοιμός is ‘uproar’, the noise and confusion of battle; ἄσπετον is ‘boundless’. Τρώεσσιν is the epic dative plural.

sentences.t:
ὡς δ’ ὅτ’ ἀριζήλη φωνή, ὅτε τ’ ἴαχε σάλπιγξ
ἄστυ περιπλομένων δηΐων ὕπο θυμοραϊστέων,
ὣς τότ’ ἀριζήλη φωνὴ γένετ’ Αἰακίδαο.
sentences.l:
As when the voice is conspicuous, when the trumpet rang out,
the town, with enemies circling it, under life-destroying ones,
so then conspicuous became the voice of Aeacus’ descendant.
sentences.i: As a voice is conspicuous when the trumpet rings out, with life-destroying enemies circling a town, so conspicuous then was the voice of Aeacus’ descendant.
sentences.n: A second simile, ὡς δ’ ὅτ’ … ὣς τότ’ ‘as when … so then’. ἀριζήλη ‘conspicuous’ (ἀρι- is an intensifier) says the voice is plainly heard; σάλπιγξ is the trumpet. δηΐων … περιπλομένων is a genitive absolute, ‘enemies circling’, with the town (ἄστυ) as the object of the participle; θυμοραϊστέων ‘life-destroying’ is the genitive plural of θυμοραϊστής, with θυμός here meaning life, and ὕπο with the genitive gives the pressure the town is under. Αἰακίδαο ‘descendant of Aeacus’ is a patronymic standing for Achilles.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ ὡς οὖν ἄϊον ὄπα χάλκεον Αἰακίδαο,
πᾶσιν ὀρίνθη θυμός·
sentences.l:
And they, when then they heard the bronze voice of Aeacus’ descendant,
in all the spirit was stirred up;
sentences.i: When they heard the bronze voice of Aeacus’ descendant, the spirit in every one of them was stirred;
sentences.n: οἳ is the Trojans (the article used as a pronoun). ἄϊον is the imperfect of ἀΐω ‘hear’, without the augment. χάλκεον ‘of bronze’ describes a loud, hard voice. πᾶσιν is ‘in them all’, and ὀρίνθη is the aorist passive of ὀρίνω ‘stir up’, the verb the house table renders ‘was stirred’.

sentences.t:
ἀτὰρ καλλίτριχες ἵπποι
ἂψ ὄχεα τρόπεον·
sentences.l:
but the fair-maned horses
turned the chariots back;
sentences.i: and the fair-maned horses turned the chariots back;
sentences.n: The horses are the subject: καλλίτριχες ‘fair-maned’ is a stock adjective for horses, translated every time. τρόπεον is the imperfect of τροπέω ‘turn’, without the augment, and ἂψ ‘back’ goes with it; ὄχεα is ‘chariots’.

sentences.t: ὄσσοντο γὰρ ἄλγεα θυμῷ.
sentences.l: for they foreboded pains in their spirit.
sentences.i: for in their spirit they foresaw pains.
sentences.n: ὄσσοντο is the imperfect middle of ὄσσομαι ‘see in the mind, foresee’, and the subject is still the horses, who sense what the Trojans will suffer. ἄλγεα ‘pains’ is the house word, and θυμῷ is the dative ‘in the spirit’.

sentences.t:
ἡνίοχοι δ’ ἔκπληγεν, ἐπεὶ ἴδον ἀκάματον πῦρ
δεινὸν ὑπὲρ κεφαλῆς μεγαθύμου Πηλεΐωνος
δαιόμενον·
sentences.i: The charioteers were astounded when they saw untiring fire, dread, blazing above the head of the great-hearted son of Peleus;
sentences.n: ἔκπληγεν is the aorist passive of ἐκπλήσσω ‘strike out of one’s wits’, with the epic ending -εν for -ησαν. ἴδον ‘saw’ has no augment. ἀκάματον ‘untiring’ is the house word for this fire, and δαιόμενον is the participle of δαίομαι ‘blaze’. μεγάθυμος ‘great-hearted’ and Πηλεΐων ‘son of Peleus’ are translated the same way every time.

sentences.t: τὸ δὲ δαῖε θεὰ γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη.
sentences.l: and this the goddess, gleaming-eyed Athena, kindled.
sentences.i: and it was the goddess, gleaming-eyed Athena, who had kindled it.
sentences.n: τὸ is the article used as a pronoun, ‘that’, meaning the fire. δαῖε ‘kindled’, the transitive verb that goes with intransitive δαιόμενον ‘blazing’, repeats ἐκ … δαῖε of line 206. θεὰ γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη is the house phrase ‘the goddess, gleaming-eyed Athena’.

sentences.t:
τρὶς μὲν ὑπὲρ τάφρου μεγάλ’ ἴαχε δῖος Ἀχιλλεύς,
τρὶς δὲ κυκήθησαν Τρῶες κλειτοί τ’ ἐπίκουροι.
sentences.l:
Three times over the ditch loudly cried out heavenly Achilles,
and three times were thrown into confusion the Trojans and famous allies.
sentences.i: Three times heavenly Achilles shouted loudly over the ditch, and three times the Trojans and their famous allies were thrown into confusion.
sentences.n: τρὶς μὲν … τρὶς δέ balances the shout and its effect, each three times. μεγάλ’ is an adverb, ‘loudly’, and ἴαχε is the unaugmented aorist of ἰάχω ‘cry out’. κυκήθησαν is the aorist passive of κυκάω ‘stir up, throw into confusion’. κλειτοί is an alternative form of κλυτοί ‘famous’, and ἐπίκουροι are ‘allies’, Trojans’ helpers.

sentences.t:
ἔνθα δὲ καὶ τότ’ ὄλοντο δυώδεκα φῶτες ἄριστοι
ἀμφὶ σφοῖς ὀχέεσσι καὶ ἔγχεσιν.
sentences.l:
And there too then perished twelve men, the best,
around their own chariots and spears.
sentences.i: And there at that time twelve of their best men perished among their own chariots and spears.
sentences.n: ὄλοντο is the unaugmented aorist of ὄλλυμι (middle) ‘perish’. δυώδεκα ‘twelve’ is Homeric for δώδεκα; φῶτες is a poetic word for ‘men’. σφοῖς ‘their own’ is the possessive ὅς (not the relative), and ἀμφί with the dative is ‘around, among’. ὀχέεσσι is an epic dative plural, and ἔγχεσιν is the dative plural of ἔγχος ‘spear’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ Ἀχαιοὶ
ἀσπασίως Πάτροκλον ὑπ’ ἐκ βελέων ἐρύσαντες
κάτθεσαν ἐν λεχέεσσι·
sentences.i: But the Achaeans gladly dragged Patroclus out from under the missiles and laid him on a bed;
sentences.n: Patroclus’ body is recovered. ὑπ’ ἐκ is ‘out from under’, and ἐρύσαντες is the aorist participle of ἐρύω ‘drag’. κάτθεσαν is κατέθεσαν with the ε dropped. λεχέεσσι is the epic dative plural of λέχος ‘bed’; here it is the bier on which the dead are laid, which the word φέρτρον names again at 236. ἀσπασίως is ‘gladly’.

sentences.t:
φίλοι δ’ ἀμφέσταν ἑταῖροι
μυρόμενοι·
sentences.l:
and dear companions stood around,
mourning;
sentences.i: and his dear companions stood around him, mourning;
sentences.n: ἀμφέσταν is ἀμφέστησαν, the aorist of ἀμφίστημι ‘stand around’, with -αν for -ησαν. φίλοι … ἑταῖροι is ‘dear companions’, and μυρόμενοι ‘mourning’ is a participle of μύρομαι.

sentences.t:
μετὰ δέ σφι ποδώκης εἵπετ’ Ἀχιλλεὺς
δάκρυα θερμὰ χέων, ἐπεὶ εἴσιδε πιστὸν ἑταῖρον
κείμενον ἐν φέρτρῳ δεδαϊγμένον ὀξέϊ χαλκῷ,
sentences.l:
and among them followed fleet-footed Achilles,
shedding hot tears, when he saw his trusty companion
lying on the bier, mangled by the sharp bronze,
sentences.i: and among them fleet-footed Achilles followed, shedding hot tears, when he saw his trusty companion lying on the bier, mangled by the sharp bronze,
sentences.n: εἵπετ’ is εἵπετο, the imperfect of ἕπομαι ‘follow’, and μετὰ … σφι is ‘among them’, with σφι the dative of the pronoun. ποδώκης ‘fleet-footed’ is the house word for this epithet. δάκρυα θερμὰ χέων ‘shedding hot tears’ is the table’s phrase (7.426). εἴσιδε ‘saw’ is the aorist of εἰσοράω. φέρτρον is a bier or litter, ‘a thing for carrying’. δεδαϊγμένον is the perfect passive participle of δαΐζω ‘cut up, mangle’, and ὀξέϊ χαλκῷ is ‘the sharp bronze’.

sentences.t:
τόν ῥ’ ἤτοι μὲν ἔπεμπε σὺν ἵπποισιν καὶ ὄχεσφιν
ἐς πόλεμον, οὐδ’ αὖτις ἐδέξατο νοστήσαντα.
sentences.l:
whom indeed he had been sending with horses and chariot
into war, and did not receive again on his return.
sentences.i: the man he had sent out to war with horses and chariot, and did not receive again on his return.
sentences.n: The relative clause belongs to πιστὸν ἑταῖρον: Achilles had sent Patroclus out and now cannot welcome him home. τόν is the article used as a relative pronoun, and ῥ’ is ῥα. ἤτοι μέν ‘truly’ is emphatic. ὄχεσφιν has the old ending -φιν and means ‘with chariot’; ἐδέξατο is the aorist of δέχομαι ‘receive’, and νοστήσαντα is the aorist participle of νοστέω ‘come home’.

sentences.t:
Ἠέλιον δ’ ἀκάμαντα βοῶπις πότνια Ἥρη
πέμψεν ἐπ’ Ὠκεανοῖο ῥοὰς ἀέκοντα νέεσθαι·
sentences.l:
And the Sun, untiring, ox-eyed lady Hera
sent to the streams of Oceanus, unwilling, to go;
sentences.i: Ox-eyed lady Hera sent the untiring Sun, unwilling, to go to the streams of Oceanus;
sentences.n: A new paragraph and a new scene: Hera ends the day. Ἠέλιον is the epic accusative of Ἠέλιος, the Sun as a god, and ἀκάμαντα ‘untiring’ is his epithet here. βοῶπις πότνια Ἥρη is the house phrase ‘ox-eyed lady Hera’ (the usual explanation is that it praises large, calm eyes). ἀέκοντα ‘unwilling’ is the accusative of ἀέκων, and νέεσθαι is the infinitive of νέομαι ‘go’. The streams of Oceanus are where the sun goes down, so the sun sets, as the next line says.

sentences.t:
ἠέλιος μὲν ἔδυ, παύσαντο δὲ δῖοι Ἀχαιοὶ
φυλόπιδος κρατερῆς καὶ ὁμοιΐου πολέμοιο.
sentences.l:
The sun set, and the heavenly Achaeans ceased
from strong battle-din and war common to all.
sentences.i: The sun set, and the heavenly Achaeans ceased from strong battle-din and from the war that is common to all.
sentences.n: Hera’s order takes effect at once. ἔδυ is the aorist of δύω ‘go down, set’. παύσαντο is an aorist middle ‘ceased’, taking the genitive of what was stopped. φυλόπιδος is the genitive of φύλοπις ‘battle-din’, and ὁμοιΐου ‘common to all’ means war shared alike by both sides, as in the house table.

sentences.t:
Τρῶες δ’ αὖθ’ ἑτέρωθεν ἀπὸ κρατερῆς ὑσμίνης
χωρήσαντες ἔλυσαν ὑφ’ ἅρμασιν ὠκέας ἵππους,
ἐς δ’ ἀγορὴν ἀγέροντο πάρος δόρποιο μέδεσθαι.
sentences.l:
And the Trojans, in turn, on the other side from strong battle
having drawn back, unyoked from the chariots the swift horses,
and to assembly they gathered before thinking of supper.
sentences.i: On the other side, the Trojans withdrew from strong battle and unyoked their swift horses from the chariots, and gathered in assembly before taking thought for supper.
sentences.n: αὖθ’ ἑτέρωθεν ‘in turn, from the other side’ turns from the Achaeans to the Trojans. χωρήσαντες is the aorist participle of χωρέω ‘withdraw’, and ὑφ’ ἅρμασιν is ‘from under the chariots’, where the horses were yoked. ἀγέροντο is the unaugmented aorist middle of ἀγείρω ‘gather’. πάρος δόρποιο μέδεσθαι is ‘before taking thought for supper’: μέδεσθαι governs the genitive.

sentences.t:
ὀρθῶν δ’ ἑσταότων ἀγορὴ γένετ’, οὐδέ τις ἔτλη
ἕζεσθαι·
sentences.l:
Standing upright was the assembly held, nor did anyone bring himself
to sit;
sentences.i: The assembly was held with everyone standing upright, and no one could bring himself to sit down;
sentences.n: ὀρθῶν … ἑσταότων is a genitive absolute, ‘with them standing upright’, and ἑσταότων is the perfect participle of ἵστημι. γένετ’ is the unaugmented aorist γένετο ‘came to be’. οὐδέ τις ἔτλη ‘no one brought himself to’ is followed here by the infinitive ἕζεσθαι ‘to sit’. Standing is a sign of the Trojans’ fear, which the next lines give.

sentences.t:
πάντας γὰρ ἔχε τρόμος, οὕνεκ’ Ἀχιλλεὺς
ἐξεφάνη, δηρὸν δὲ μάχης ἐπέπαυτ’ ἀλεγεινῆς.
sentences.l:
for a trembling held them all, because Achilles
had appeared, and for long from grievous fighting had ceased.
sentences.i: for a trembling took hold of them all, because Achilles had appeared, after long ceasing from grievous fighting.
sentences.n: τρόμος ‘trembling’ is the house word, and ἔχε is the unaugmented imperfect ‘held’, which English puts as ‘took hold of’ in the readable line. οὕνεκ’ is οὕνεκα ‘because’. ἐξεφάνη is the aorist passive of ἐκφαίνω ‘show forth’, here ‘appeared’. ἐπέπαυτ’ is ἐπέπαυτο, the pluperfect middle of παύω, with the augment and the reduplication, ‘had stopped’, and it takes the genitive μάχης. ἀλεγεινῆς ‘grievous’ is the house word.

sentences.t:
τοῖσι δὲ Πουλυδάμας πεπνυμένος ἦρχ’ ἀγορεύειν
Πανθοΐδης·
sentences.l:
And among them Polydamas, prudent, began to speak,
Panthous’-son;
sentences.i: And prudent Polydamas, son of Panthous, was the first to speak among them;
sentences.n: Πουλυδάμας is the Homeric spelling of Polydamas. ἦρχ’ ἀγορεύειν is ‘was the first to speak’ (ἦρχε is the imperfect of ἄρχω), and the pattern is the table’s whole-line speech introduction. πεπνυμένος ‘prudent’ is his stock epithet, translated every time. Πανθοΐδης is a patronymic, ‘son of Panthous’, formed like Ἀτρεΐδης.

sentences.t: ὃ γὰρ οἶος ὅρα πρόσσω καὶ ὀπίσσω·
sentences.l: for he alone looked forward and backward;
sentences.i: for he alone looked both forward and back;
sentences.n: ὅ is the article used as a pronoun, ‘he’. ὅρα is the imperfect of ὁράω without the augment (Attic ἑώρα). πρόσσω καὶ ὀπίσσω is ‘forward and backward’; the phrase is usually taken to mean that he could see both what was coming and what lay behind, but the Greek says only ‘forward and backward’.

sentences.t:
Ἕκτορι δ’ ἦεν ἑταῖρος, ἰῇ δ’ ἐν νυκτὶ γένοντο,
ἀλλ’ ὃ μὲν ἂρ μύθοισιν, ὃ δ’ ἔγχεϊ πολλὸν ἐνίκα·
sentences.l:
And to Hector he was a companion, and in one night they came to be,
but the one in words, the other with the spear far surpassed;
sentences.i: He was Hector’s companion, and they were born on the same night; but the one was far the better with words, the other with the spear;
sentences.n: ἦεν is the epic imperfect of εἰμί, ‘was’. ἰῇ is the feminine dative of εἷς ‘one’ (Attic μιᾷ), and γένοντο ‘came to be’ has no augment; the sense is ‘were born’. ὃ μὲν … ὃ δέ is ‘the one … the other’, and ἐνίκα is the imperfect of νικάω ‘surpass’, with πολλόν ‘by much’, so that each is said to have been far the better at his own skill. ἔγχεϊ is the epic dative of ἔγχος ‘spear’.

sentences.t: ὅ σφιν ἐϋφρονέων ἀγορήσατο καὶ μετέειπεν·
sentences.l: he, well-disposed in mind toward them, addressed-the-assembly and spoke among them:
sentences.i: with kindly intent toward them he addressed the assembly and spoke among them:
sentences.n: This is the same speech introduction as at 7.326, so the English is the same. ὅ is the article used as a pronoun, ‘he’; σφιν is ‘to them’ and ἐϋφρονέων ‘kindly-minded’ (ἐΰ ‘well’ + φρονέω). ἀγορήσατο is the aorist of ἀγοράομαι ‘address an assembly’, and μετέειπεν is ‘spoke among them’. The speech begins in the next line.

sentences.t: ἀμφὶ μάλα φράζεσθε φίλοι·
sentences.l: “Consider well on all sides, friends;
sentences.i: “Think it over from every side, friends;
sentences.n: Polydamas speaks. φράζεσθε is the present imperative middle of φράζομαι ‘consider’, and ἀμφὶ μάλα is ‘thoroughly, on every side’, with ἀμφί here an adverb. φίλοι ‘friends’ is a vocative. The unit ends at the first stop.

sentences.t:
κέλομαι γὰρ ἔγωγε
ἄστυδε νῦν ἰέναι, μὴ μίμνειν ἠῶ δῖαν
ἐν πεδίῳ παρὰ νηυσίν·
sentences.i: for I at least bid us go to the town now, and not wait for heavenly dawn on the plain by the ships;
sentences.n: κέλομαι ‘I urge’ takes infinitives, with ‘us’ understood as their subject. ἔγωγε is ἐγώ with the emphatic -γε, ‘I at least’. ἄστυδε ‘to the town’ has the suffix -δε of direction, and ἰέναι is the infinitive of εἶμι ‘go’. μίμνειν ‘to wait for’ takes ἠῶ δῖαν ‘heavenly dawn’, with δῖαν the stock epithet, translated every time.

sentences.t: ἑκὰς δ’ ἀπὸ τείχεός εἰμεν.
sentences.l: and far from the wall we are.
sentences.i: we are far from the wall.
sentences.n: εἰμεν is the epic form of ἐσμέν ‘we are’. ἑκὰς … ἀπό means ‘far from’ with the genitive τείχεος, the epic genitive of τεῖχος. The wall is the wall of Troy, which the Trojans have left behind on the plain.

sentences.t:
ὄφρα μὲν οὗτος ἀνὴρ Ἀγαμέμνονι μήνιε δίῳ
τόφρα δὲ ῥηΐτεροι πολεμίζειν ἦσαν Ἀχαιοί·
sentences.l:
As long as this man was wrathful at heavenly Agamemnon,
so long were the Achaeans easier to fight;
sentences.i: As long as this man was in wrath at heavenly Agamemnon, so long the Achaeans were easier to fight;
sentences.n: ‘This man’ (οὗτος ἀνήρ) is Achilles. ὄφρα … τόφρα is ‘as long as … so long’. μήνιε is the imperfect of μηνίω ‘be wrathful’, from μῆνις ‘wrath’, and it takes the dative Ἀγαμέμνονι. ῥηΐτεροι is the comparative of ῥηΐδιος ‘easy’ (Attic ῥᾴδιος), and with πολεμίζειν ‘to fight’ it means ‘easier to fight’. δίῳ is the stock epithet ‘heavenly’.

sentences.t:
χαίρεσκον γὰρ ἔγωγε θοῇς ἐπὶ νηυσὶν ἰαύων
ἐλπόμενος νῆας αἱρησέμεν ἀμφιελίσσας.
sentences.l:
for I used to rejoice, I at least, sleeping by the swift ships,
hoping to take the both-sides-curving ships.
sentences.i: for I at least used to be glad to sleep by the swift ships, hoping to take the ships curved on both sides.
sentences.n: χαίρεσκον is an iterative imperfect (the suffix -σκ- marks a repeated action), ‘used to rejoice’. ἰαύων ‘sleeping, passing the night’ and ἐλπόμενος ‘hoping’ are participles, and ἐλπόμενος takes the future infinitive αἱρησέμεν, with the ending -έμεν for -ειν, ‘to take’. θοῇς ‘swift’ and ἀμφιελίσσας ‘curved on both sides’ are the house renderings; the ships are the Achaeans’.

sentences.t: νῦν δ’ αἰνῶς δείδοικα ποδώκεα Πηλεΐωνα·
sentences.l: But now dreadfully I fear the fleet-footed son of Peleus;
sentences.i: But now I am dreadfully afraid of the fleet-footed son of Peleus;
sentences.n: δείδοικα is a perfect with present sense, ‘I fear’, and takes the accusative. αἰνῶς ‘dreadfully’. ποδώκεα Πηλεΐωνα is ‘the fleet-footed son of Peleus’: ποδώκης (πούς + ὠκύς) is the house ‘fleet-footed’, and Πηλεΐων is the patronymic of Achilles.

sentences.t:
οἷος κείνου θυμὸς ὑπέρβιος, οὐκ ἐθελήσει
μίμνειν ἐν πεδίῳ, ὅθι περ Τρῶες καὶ Ἀχαιοὶ
ἐν μέσῳ ἀμφότεροι μένος Ἄρηος δατέονται,
ἀλλὰ περὶ πτόλιός τε μαχήσεται ἠδὲ γυναικῶν.
sentences.l:
Such is that man’s exceeding spirit, he will not be willing
to wait on the plain, where Trojans and Achaeans
in the middle, both of them, share out the might of Ares,
but will fight for the city and for women.
sentences.i: That man’s spirit is so exceeding that he will not be willing to wait on the plain, where Trojans and Achaeans alike, in the middle, share out the might of war between them, but he will fight for the city and for the women.
sentences.n: οἷος … θυμὸς ὑπέρβιος is ‘such an exceeding spirit’, and ὑπέρβιος ‘exceeding’ is built from ὑπέρ ‘beyond’ and βίη ‘force’. κείνου is ἐκείνου ‘of that man’, and ἐθελήσει is the future of ἐθέλω. ὅθι περ is ‘just where’, and ἐν μέσῳ ἀμφότεροι ‘both in the middle’. δατέονται is the uncontracted δατέομαι ‘divide, share out’: the two sides share out the might (μένος) of Ares, who stands for war, as men share a portion. πτόλις is the Homeric form of πόλις, and γυναικῶν is ‘women’, wives included.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἴομεν προτὶ ἄστυ, πίθεσθέ μοι·
sentences.l: But let us go toward the town, obey me;
sentences.i: Instead, let us go to the town; take my advice;
sentences.n: ἴομεν is the short-vowel subjunctive of εἶμι, used as an exhortation, ‘let us go’ (= ἴωμεν). προτί is the epic form of πρός ‘toward’. πίθεσθε is the aorist imperative middle of πείθω, ‘obey’, with the dative μοι.

sentences.t: ὧδε γὰρ ἔσται·
sentences.l: for thus it will be:
sentences.i: for this is how it will be:
sentences.n: ὧδε ‘thus’ points forward to the picture Polydamas now draws, and ἔσται is the future ‘will be’.

sentences.t:
νῦν μὲν νὺξ ἀπέπαυσε ποδώκεα Πηλεΐωνα
ἀμβροσίη·
sentences.l:
Now night has stopped the fleet-footed son of Peleus,
the ambrosial night;
sentences.i: For now the ambrosial night has stopped the fleet-footed son of Peleus;
sentences.n: νῦν μέν ‘for now’ prepares the contrast with tomorrow (αὔριον) in the next unit. ἀπέπαυσε is a transitive aorist, ‘stopped’. ἀμβροσίη ‘ambrosial’ is the house word, as in ἀμβροσίη νύξ, ‘the ambrosial night’ (2.57), and the word is held back to the start of the second line, after νύξ and the verb, for emphasis.

sentences.t:
εἰ δ’ ἄμμε κιχήσεται ἐνθάδ’ ἐόντας
αὔριον ὁρμηθεὶς σὺν τεύχεσιν, εὖ νύ τις αὐτὸν
γνώσεται·
sentences.i: but if he finds us still here tomorrow when he sets out in his armour, someone will come to know him well;
sentences.n: ἄμμε is the Aeolic-looking form of ἡμέας ‘us’. κιχήσεται is a future (or short-vowel subjunctive) of κιχάνω ‘find, reach’ after εἰ. ἐόντας is the participle of εἰμί, ‘being’, and ὁρμηθείς the aorist passive participle of ὁρμάομαι ‘set out’. εὖ νύ τις αὐτὸν γνώσεται, ‘someone will know him well’, is a threat: whoever meets him will learn what he is.

sentences.t:
ἀσπασίως γὰρ ἀφίξεται Ἴλιον ἱρὴν
ὅς κε φύγῃ, πολλοὺς δὲ κύνες καὶ γῦπες ἔδονται
Τρώων·
sentences.i: for whoever escapes will gladly reach sacred Ilium, and dogs and vultures will eat many of the Trojans;
sentences.n: ἀφίξεται is the future of ἀφικνέομαι ‘arrive’, and ὅς κε φύγῃ is ‘whoever may flee’, a general relative clause with κε and the aorist subjunctive. ἀσπασίως ‘gladly’ is grim here, since only a survivor will reach the city. πολλούς is the object of ἔδονται ‘will eat’ (future of ἔδω), and Τρώων is the genitive of the group, ‘many of the Trojans’. Ἴλιον ἱρήν is the table’s ‘sacred Ilium’.

sentences.t: αἲ γὰρ δή μοι ἀπ’ οὔατος ὧδε γένοιτο.
sentences.l: O that, indeed, away from my ear thus it might happen.
sentences.i: Would that this might be kept far from my hearing!
sentences.n: αἲ γάρ with the optative γένοιτο is a wish, ‘would that’. ἀπ’ οὔατος means ‘away from the ear’, and the idiom is taken to mean ‘far from my hearing’, so that Polydamas does not wish to hear of such a thing; the exact force of ὧδε ‘thus’ is not certain.

sentences.t:
εἰ δ’ ἂν ἐμοῖς ἐπέεσσι πιθώμεθα κηδόμενοί περ,
νύκτα μὲν εἰν ἀγορῇ σθένος ἕξομεν, ἄστυ δὲ πύργοι
ὑψηλαί τε πύλαι σανίδες τ’ ἐπὶ τῇς ἀραρυῖαι
μακραὶ ἐΰξεστοι ἐζευγμέναι εἰρύσσονται·
sentences.l:
But if we obey my words, troubled though we are,
through the night in the assembly we shall have strength, and the town, the towers
and high gates, and doors fitted to them,
tall, well-smoothed, joined, will protect.
sentences.i: But if we are persuaded by my words, worried as we are, then through the night we shall keep our strength in the assembly, and the towers, the high gates and the doors fitted to them, tall, well-smoothed and joined, will protect the town;
sentences.n: εἰ … ἂν … πιθώμεθα is εἰ with the aorist subjunctive, ‘if we obey’, with ἐμοῖς ἐπέεσσι the epic dative ‘my words’. κηδόμενοί περ is ‘though we are troubled’. σθένος ἕξομεν, ‘we shall have strength’, says the army, kept together in the assembly through the night, stays strong. ἄστυ is the object of εἰρύσσονται ‘will protect’, whose subjects are the towers, the gates and the doors. ἐπὶ τῇς ἀραρυῖαι is ‘fitted upon them’ (the doors on the gates); σανίδες is ‘doors’, ἀραρυῖαι the perfect participle of ἀραρίσκω ‘fit’, ἐΰξεστοι ‘well-smoothed’, and ἐζευγμέναι the perfect passive participle of ζεύγνυμι ‘join’.

sentences.t:
πρῶϊ δ’ ὑπηοῖοι σὺν τεύχεσι θωρηχθέντες
στησόμεθ’ ἂμ πύργους·
sentences.l:
and early in the morning, at dawn, in our armour armed,
we shall take our stand along the towers;
sentences.i: and early in the morning, at daybreak, armed in our armour, we shall take our stand along the towers;
sentences.n: The first line is word for word 8.530, and it is repeated by Hector at 303, so the English is the same each time. θωρηχθέντες is the aorist passive participle of θωρήσσω ‘arm’. στησόμεθ’ is the future middle of ἵστημι, ‘we shall take our stand’, and ἂμ πύργους is ἀνὰ πύργους ‘up along the towers’, with the ν assimilated to the following π.

sentences.t:
τῷ δ’ ἄλγιον, αἴ κ’ ἐθέλῃσιν
ἐλθὼν ἐκ νηῶν περὶ τείχεος ἄμμι μάχεσθαι.
sentences.l:
and the more painful for him, if he is willing,
having come from the ships, to fight with us around the wall.
sentences.i: and the more painful for him, if he is willing to come from the ships and fight us around the wall.
sentences.n: τῷ ‘for him’ is the article used as a pronoun, in the dative, and ἄλγιον ‘the more painful’ is a comparative; the verb ‘it will be’ is left out. αἴ κ’ ἐθέλῃσιν is ‘if he is willing’, with κε and the subjunctive. ἄμμι is ἡμῖν ‘to us’, and τείχεος is the epic genitive of τεῖχος. Hector will turn this phrase back on Achilles at 306.

sentences.t:
ἂψ πάλιν εἶσ’ ἐπὶ νῆας, ἐπεί κ’ ἐριαύχενας ἵππους
παντοίου δρόμου ἄσῃ ὑπὸ πτόλιν ἠλασκάζων·
sentences.l:
Back again he will go to the ships, when he has sated his strong-necked horses
with every kind of running, roaming under the city;
sentences.i: He will go back again to the ships once he has given his strong-necked horses their fill of every kind of running as he roams about beneath the city;
sentences.n: εἶσ’ is εἶσι, the present of εἶμι used as a future, ‘he will go’, and ἂψ πάλιν ‘back again’ doubles the idea. ἐπεί κ’ … ἄσῃ is ‘when he has …’, with the aorist subjunctive of ἄω ‘satiate’, whose object is the horses and whose genitive παντοίου δρόμου says with what. ἠλασκάζων ‘roaming’ is the participle of ἠλασκάζω. ἐριαύχενας ‘strong-necked’ follows the house rendering; the exact sense of ἐρι- is not known.

sentences.t:
εἴσω δ’ οὔ μιν θυμὸς ἐφορμηθῆναι ἐάσει,
οὐδέ ποτ’ ἐκπέρσει·
sentences.l:
And within his spirit will not allow him to rush,
nor will he ever sack it;
sentences.i: but his spirit will not let him dash inside, and he will never sack the town;
sentences.n: εἴσω ‘inside’. The θυμός that ‘will not allow’ him is Achilles’ own spirit, and Polydamas’ argument is that he will not force his way into the city. ἐφορμηθῆναι is the aorist passive infinitive of ἐφορμάω ‘rush at’, and ἐάσει the future of ἐάω ‘allow’. ἐκπέρσει is the future of ἐκπέρθω ‘sack’, with the town as its unstated object.

sentences.t: πρίν μιν κύνες ἀργοὶ ἔδονται.
sentences.l: before that, the swift dogs will eat him.”
sentences.i: the swift dogs will eat him first.”
sentences.n: πρίν with a future verb means ‘before that’, so the sense is that the dogs will eat him first. κύνες ἀργοί is ‘swift dogs’, the house rendering: ἀργός means ‘swift’ or ‘white’, and which is meant is disputed. ἔδονται is the future of ἔδω ‘eat’, as in 271, and μιν is ‘him’.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἄρ’ ὑπόδρα ἰδὼν προσέφη κορυθαίολος Ἕκτωρ·
sentences.l: Him then with a scowl looking addressed Hector of the glancing helmet:
sentences.i: Then Hector of the glancing helmet, looking at him with a scowl, spoke to him:
sentences.n: This is the same line as 12.230, so the English is the same. τὸν is the article used as a pronoun, ‘him’, meaning Polydamas, and ὑπόδρα ἰδών means ‘looking’ with a scowl; the derivation of ὑπόδρα is not certain. κορυθαίολος ‘of the glancing helmet’ is Hector’s stock epithet, translated every time.

sentences.t:
Πουλυδάμα σὺ μὲν οὐκέτ’ ἐμοὶ φίλα ταῦτ’ ἀγορεύεις,
ὃς κέλεαι κατὰ ἄστυ ἀλήμεναι αὖτις ἰόντας.
sentences.l:
“Polydamas, you no longer say these things dear to me,
you who bid us crowd together in the town, going back again.
sentences.i: “Polydamas, what you say is no longer dear to me, you who tell us to go back and crowd together inside the town.
sentences.n: Hector answers. φίλα ‘dear’ is ‘pleasing’, and ταῦτα ‘these things’ is the object of ἀγορεύεις. ὃς κέλεαι is ‘you who urge’, with κέλεαι the uncontracted form of κέλῃ. ἀλήμεναι is an aorist passive infinitive tied to εἴλω, ‘to be crowded together’, and ἰόντας ‘going’ agrees with ‘us’, understood. Πουλυδάμα is the vocative.

sentences.t: ἦ οὔ πω κεκόρησθε ἐελμένοι ἔνδοθι πύργων;
sentences.l: Surely you have not yet had your fill of being hemmed in within the towers?
sentences.i: Have you not yet had your fill of being hemmed in inside the towers?
sentences.n: ἦ opens a question, and the Greek question mark ends the unit. κεκόρησθε is the perfect middle of κορέννυμι ‘satisfy’, ‘you have had your fill’. ἐελμένοι is the perfect passive participle of εἴλω ‘hem in’, the verb tied to ἀλήμεναι in the line before. ἔνδοθι is ‘inside’.

sentences.t:
πρὶν μὲν γὰρ Πριάμοιο πόλιν μέροπες ἄνθρωποι
πάντες μυθέσκοντο πολύχρυσον πολύχαλκον·
sentences.l:
For formerly the city of Priam all speech-dividing men
used to call rich in gold, rich in bronze;
sentences.i: For formerly all men of articulate speech used to call Priam’s city rich in gold and rich in bronze;
sentences.n: The meaning of μέροπες is not known; the ancient explanation, ‘having divided (that is, articulate) speech’, is followed, as in the Odyssey. μυθέσκοντο is an iterative imperfect of μυθέομαι ‘say’, ‘used to say’. πολύχρυσον ‘rich in gold’ and πολύχαλκον ‘rich in bronze’ are built the same way. Πριάμοιο is the epic genitive of Priam.

sentences.t:
νῦν δὲ δὴ ἐξαπόλωλε δόμων κειμήλια καλά,
πολλὰ δὲ δὴ Φρυγίην καὶ Μῃονίην ἐρατεινὴν
κτήματα περνάμεν’ ἵκει, ἐπεὶ μέγας ὠδύσατο Ζεύς.
sentences.l:
But now have perished utterly the fair treasures of our houses,
and many, to Phrygia and lovely Maeonia,
possessions, being sold, come, since great Zeus grew angry.
sentences.i: But now the fair treasures of our houses have utterly perished, and many possessions are going off, sold, to Phrygia and lovely Maeonia, since great Zeus grew angry.
sentences.n: ἐξαπόλωλε is the perfect of ἐξαπόλλυμι ‘perish utterly’, and it is singular because neuter plurals take a singular verb: so too ἵκει, for κτήματα ‘possessions’. κειμήλια is ‘treasures’, things stored away. περνάμεν’ is the participle περνάμενα, from πέρνημι ‘sell’, in the passive sense ‘being sold’; Phrygia and Maeonia are lands of Asia Minor, and Maeonia is Lydia. ὠδύσατο is the aorist of ὀδύσσομαι ‘be angry’.

sentences.t:
νῦν δ’ ὅτε πέρ μοι ἔδωκε Κρόνου πάϊς ἀγκυλομήτεω
κῦδος ἀρέσθ’ ἐπὶ νηυσί, θαλάσσῃ τ’ ἔλσαι Ἀχαιούς,
νήπιε μηκέτι ταῦτα νοήματα φαῖν’ ἐνὶ δήμῳ·
sentences.i: But now, just when the son of Cronus of crooked cunning has granted me to win glory at the ships and to hem the Achaeans in against the sea, foolish one, no longer show such thoughts among the people;
sentences.n: νῦν δ’ ὅτε πέρ is ‘but now, just when’. Κρόνου πάϊς, ‘son of Cronus’, is Zeus, here with Cronus’ own epithet ἀγκυλομήτεω ‘of crooked cunning’, in the genitive with Κρόνου. ἀρέσθαι is the aorist infinitive middle of αἴρω, ‘to win’, in κῦδος ἀρέσθαι ‘to win glory’. ἔλσαι ‘to hem in’ is the aorist infinitive of εἴλω, the verb of ἐελμένοι above. νήπιε is a vocative, ‘foolish one’, and φαῖν’ is the imperative φαῖνε ‘show’. δήμῳ is the dative of δῆμος ‘people’.

sentences.t: οὐ γάρ τις Τρώων ἐπιπείσεται·
sentences.l: for no one of the Trojans will obey;
sentences.i: for no one of the Trojans will obey you;
sentences.n: ἐπιπείσεται is the future of ἐπιπείθομαι ‘obey’, with ‘you’ left unsaid. The two sentences both begin with οὐ γάρ ‘for not’: the first says what the Trojans will do, the second what Hector will not allow.

sentences.t: οὐ γὰρ ἐάσω.
sentences.l: for I will not allow it.
sentences.i: for I will not allow it.
sentences.n: ἐάσω is the future of ἐάω ‘allow’. Hector sets his own refusal beside the army’s.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἄγεθ’ ὡς ἂν ἐγὼ εἴπω, πειθώμεθα πάντες.
sentences.l: But come, as I may say, let us obey, all of us;
sentences.i: But come, let us all do as I say;
sentences.n: This is the same line as 2.139, where it has the same English (the edition here prints a comma after εἴπω and a full stop at the end, where 2.139 has no comma and a raised point). ἄγεθ’ is ἄγετε ‘come’. ὡς ἂν ἐγὼ εἴπω is ‘as I may say’, with ἄν and the aorist subjunctive, and πειθώμεθα is a hortative subjunctive, ‘let us obey’.

sentences.t:
νῦν μὲν δόρπον ἕλεσθε κατὰ στρατὸν ἐν τελέεσσι,
καὶ φυλακῆς μνήσασθε, καὶ ἐγρήγορθε ἕκαστος·
sentences.l:
Now take your supper throughout the army, in your companies,
and be mindful of the watch, and be wakeful, each one;
sentences.i: For now, take your supper throughout the army, company by company, and be mindful of the watch, and keep awake, each one of you;
sentences.n: The same call to supper and watch stands at 7.370–371, with ‘through the city, as before’ in place of ‘throughout the army, in your companies’; the second line is word for word the same, and so is its English. δόρπον ἕλεσθε is ‘take your supper’, with ἕλεσθε the aorist imperative middle of αἱρέω. τελέεσσι is the epic dative plural of τέλος in the sense ‘company, unit’. φυλακῆς takes the genitive after μνήσασθε ‘be mindful of’, and ἐγρήγορθε is the perfect imperative of ἐγείρω, ‘be awake’.

sentences.t:
Τρώων δ’ ὃς κτεάτεσσιν ὑπερφιάλως ἀνιάζει,
συλλέξας λαοῖσι δότω καταδημοβορῆσαι·
sentences.l:
And whichever of the Trojans is distressed beyond measure over his possessions,
let him gather them and give them to the people to eat up in common;
sentences.i: And any Trojan who is distressed beyond measure over his possessions, let him gather them and give them to the people to eat up;
sentences.n: ὃς … ἀνιάζει is a general relative clause, ‘whoever is distressed’, and ἀνιάζει is used here intransitively. ὑπερφιάλως is ‘beyond measure’, and κτεάτεσσιν the epic dative plural of κτέαρ ‘possession’. συλλέξας is ‘having gathered’, and δότω is the third-person imperative of δίδωμι. καταδημοβορῆσαι is an unusual compound, built from κατα- ‘down, up’, δῆμος ‘people’ and a root meaning ‘devour’, so ‘to eat up in common, among the people’; its exact make-up is not certain.

sentences.t: τῶν τινὰ βέλτερόν ἐστιν ἐπαυρέμεν ἤ περ Ἀχαιούς.
sentences.l: of them someone it is better to have the benefit than the Achaeans.
sentences.i: It is better that someone among them should have the benefit of it than the Achaeans.
sentences.n: τῶν τινά ‘someone of them’ refers to the people just named. βέλτερον is ‘better’ (Attic βέλτιον), and ἐπαυρέμεν is the aorist infinitive of ἐπαυρίσκω ‘have the benefit’, with the thing enjoyed left unsaid. ἤ περ is ‘than’.

sentences.t:
πρῶϊ δ’ ὑπηοῖοι σὺν τεύχεσι θωρηχθέντες
νηυσὶν ἔπι γλαφυρῇσιν ἐγείρομεν ὀξὺν Ἄρηα.
sentences.l:
and early in the morning, at dawn, in our armour armed,
at the hollow ships we shall rouse sharp Ares.
sentences.i: And early in the morning, at daybreak, armed in our armour, we shall rouse keen battle at the hollow ships.
sentences.n: Line 303 is the same as 277, and the pair 303–304 is word for word 8.530–531, so the English is the same. Where Polydamas used these words to stand on the towers, Hector uses them to attack the ships. ἐγείρομεν is a subjunctive with the force of a future, ‘we shall rouse’. ὀξὺν Ἄρηα is ‘sharp Ares’ in the literal English and ‘keen battle’ in the readable English, with Ares standing for war.

sentences.t:
εἰ δ’ ἐτεὸν παρὰ ναῦφιν ἀνέστη δῖος Ἀχιλλεύς,
ἄλγιον αἴ κ’ ἐθέλῃσι τῷ ἔσσεται·
sentences.l:
But if truly beside the ships heavenly Achilles has risen up,
the more painful will it be for him, if he is willing;
sentences.i: But if heavenly Achilles has really risen up beside the ships, it will be the more painful for him if he is willing;
sentences.n: ἐτεόν is ‘truly’, and ναῦφιν has the old ending -φιν, here ‘beside the ships’. ἀνέστη is the aorist of ἀνίστημι ‘has risen up’. ἄλγιον … τῷ ἔσσεται, ‘the more painful for him’, and αἴ κ’ ἐθέλῃσι ‘if he is willing’ turn Polydamas’ words of 278 back on Achilles. What he must be willing to do is left unsaid.

sentences.t:
οὔ μιν ἔγωγε
φεύξομαι ἐκ πολέμοιο δυσηχέος, ἀλλὰ μάλ’ ἄντην
στήσομαι, ἤ κε φέρῃσι μέγα κράτος, ἦ κε φεροίμην.
sentences.l:
I at least shall not flee him
out of the ill-sounding war, but right face to face
I shall stand, whether he carry off great strength, or I carry it off.
sentences.i: I at least shall not run from him out of the ill-sounding war, but shall stand against him face to face, whether he carries off great strength or I do.
sentences.n: μιν is ‘him’, the object of φεύξομαι ‘I shall flee’. δυσηχέος ‘ill-sounding’ goes with πολέμοιο, and ἄντην is ‘face to face’. στήσομαι is the future middle of ἵστημι, ‘I shall make my stand’. ἤ κε φέρῃσι … ἦ κε φεροίμην is ‘whether he may carry off … or I may’, with the old subjunctive ending -σι and then the optative. κράτος is ‘strength’, the house word, which here includes the upper hand.

sentences.t: ξυνὸς Ἐνυάλιος, καί τε κτανέοντα κατέκτα.
sentences.l: Common is Enyalius, and him who is about to kill he kills.”
sentences.i: Enyalius is common to all, and he kills even the man who is about to kill.”
sentences.n: Ἐνυάλιος is a name of the war-god, used here for war itself. ξυνός is ‘common, shared’ (= κοινός), so war is impartial. καί τε … κατέκτα: τε marks a general truth, and the aorist κατέκτα (aorist of κατακτείνω ‘kill’) states what always happens; κτανέοντα is the participle ‘being about to kill’.
